 A Ship Captain’s Hormuz Danger Pay Blew Past Social Security’s $24,480 Limit but He Could Still Collect After His Final Voyage
 A tanker captain running the Strait of Hormuz earns more in one month than Social Security allows in a full year, yet a little-known monthly rule could still put a check in his mailbox before the calendar flips to January.
 By Gerelyn Terzo 
 Published October 19, 2026, 5:30am ET · 4 min read 
 The Full Benefits Desk desk. Editor: Gerelyn Terzo .
 𝕏 
 f 
 ⧉ 
 Quick Read
 A special first-year retirement rule lets retirees collect full monthly checks whenever wages stay at or below $2,040, regardless of total annual earnings.
 Pre-retirement Hormuz wages don't affect post-retirement checks. Only income earned after stepping ashore determines which monthly benefits get withheld.
 At full retirement age, Social Security credits withheld months as higher future payments, and 2026 Hormuz earnings could replace a weaker year in his top 35.

 Tanker captains running the Strait of Hormuz can earn $100,000 a month, plus a $50,000 bonus for each trip, the Financial Times reported. Their regular pay is about $15,000 a month.
 Picture a 63-year-old American captain whose wages are covered by U.S. Social Security, who signs on for one last string of Hormuz shuttle runs and has his best year ever. He steps ashore for good in late August and wants his benefits to start in September, but his worry is that he has already earned several times the year’s earnings limit. Does he have to wait until January?
 One Hormuz Month Could Wipe Out a Full Year of Checks
 If you’re under full retirement age (FRA) for all of 2026, Social Security deducts $1 for every $2 you earn above $24,480.
 Even one $100,000 month produces $37,760 in potential withholding under the annual formula. That would be enough to wipe out every benefit payable to him that year without the special monthly rule.
 What saves him is a special rule for the first year of retirement. Social Security will pay a full check for any whole month it considers you retired, “regardless of your yearly earnings.” If you’re below the age for full benefits all year, a month counts as retired when your wages are $2,040 or less and you did no substantial self-employment work.
 His Life After the Final Voyage Decides Every Check
 Look at his year one month at a time:
 January through August: He earns Hormuz pay and hasn’t claimed benefits, so those huge wages have no effect on the months after he retires. Social Security generally counts wages in the month you earn them, so a trip bonus for an August transit that arrives in September should count as August pay.
 September through December: Say he takes a part-time job at the port paying $1,500 a month. Every month stays under $2,040, so he gets all four checks. That’s $8,000 on a $2,000 benefit.
 One busy month: If a shore job pays him $2,500 in November, November doesn’t count as a retired month and that check can be held back. September, October and December are paid as normal.
 Consulting: If he works for himself, maybe screening crews for a shipowner, the hours he puts in matter more than the money. Social Security counts it as substantial if he spends more than 45 hours a month on the business, or between 15 and 45 hours in a highly skilled field. A ship captain’s know-how could easily be judged highly skilled, so 20 hours of advising in a month could cost him that month’s check.
 His Big Year Can Still Raise His Future Check
 At full retirement age (FRA), Social Security adjusts his monthly benefit to credit months when checks were withheld. That means larger future payments, not a refund of the withheld dollars. His final working year could also raise his benefit if it replaces a weaker year among his highest 35. But only earnings up to the 2026 cap of $184,500 enter that calculation. Any increase from his 2026 earnings would be effective January 2027.
 Taxes come next. The IRS adds half of his benefits to his other income, and once that total tops a set base amount, part of his benefits may be taxable . With Hormuz pay on his 2026 return, he should expect part of his fall checks to be taxed.
 As of early October, the 2027 cost-of-living increase is on track for 3.5%, which will raise his check in the new year.
 Decide These Points Before He Files
 First, make sure his sea pay was actually covered by U.S. Social Security. Many mariners work for foreign-flagged owners, and Social Security says different rules apply to people below the age for full benefits who work outside the United States. Checking his earnings record now heads off surprises later.
 Second, keep proof of his last working month: discharge papers, his final payroll date and the day he left the ship, and keep in mind that the monthly rule only covers his first year of retirement. Beginning in 2027, only his total pay for the year will count against the limit, so going back to sea, even briefly, will work very differently. Phasing out of work like this comes with its own tax traps, which we laid out in a free semi-retirement playbook . His last voyage may have delivered his biggest payday. It does not have to delay his first Social Security benefit.
